findings.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked_emails feature ships with no writer anywhere in this diff: no admin controller, API endpoint, rake task, or seed path exists to create BlockedEmail records, so the only way to populate the table is manual SQL against the production database. Operators who enable this feature cannot actually block any email — the entire block list stays empty and EmailValidator's BlockedEmail branch is dead code until someone hand-inserts rows, defeating the stated purpose of the PR.

[ADVISORY] should_block? is called from User validation on every email validation and unconditionally performs a write (record.save, which itself triggers a uniqueness-validation SELECT plus an UPDATE) as a side effect of what is supposed to be a read-only check. Every signup and email-change validation incurs an extra query pair against blocked_emails on the registration hot path, and because record.save's return value is ignored, a failed save (e.g., a uniqueness race from a concurrent insert) silently drops the stats update with no error raised.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first performs an exact, case-sensitive match, so a blocked address can be bypassed by any case variation (e.g., blocked 'bad@spamclub.com' does not match 'Bad@SpamClub.com'). An attacker who learns an address is blocked signs up with different letter casing, should_block? returns false, and the block is silently defeated — the feature's core guarantee fails on its first adversarial input.

[ADVISORY] The whitelist/blacklist domain-restriction branches in EmailValidator (the logic moved out of app/models/user.rb) have no test coverage in this diff — email_validator_spec.rb stubs should_block? and exercises only the blocked-email branch, leaving both email_in_restriction_setting? paths and the interaction where a domain error suppresses the blocked-email check untested. A regression in the domain restriction logic (e.g., the regex escaping or the elsif ordering between whitelist and blacklist) would silently allow blacklisted domains or reject whitelisted ones with no failing spec, regressing behavior that previously existed in user.rb without any guard.

[BUG] The blocked_emails feature ships with no writer anywhere in the diff — no admin controller, route, UI, rake task, or seed path exists to create a BlockedEmail record, so the table can never be populated. Operators cannot actually block any email: EmailValidator's BlockedEmail.should_block?(value) (lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13) always finds no record and returns false, making the headline feature of this PR ('comprehensive email validation for blocked users') inert until a future change adds a management path. The PR's core acceptance criterion — an admin can block an email address and signup is rejected — is silently unmet.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? matches with `BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` — an exact, case-sensitive SQL equality in PostgreSQL — so a signup email differing only in case from the blocked entry is not matched, and nothing in the diff downcases either side. An admin who blocks 'bad@spamclub.com' does not block 'Bad@Spamclub.com' or 'BAD@SPAMCLUB.COM': should_block? returns false and registration succeeds. The same case-sensitivity applies to the model's `validates :email, uniqueness: true` (line 4), so an admin adding variants one at a time gets no protection against the variants they haven't thought of. The block is trivially bypassable.

[BUG] The client pushes the email into rejectedEmails on ANY email error — `result.errors.email` is truthy for uniqueness ('has already been taken'), whitelist/blacklist ('not_allowed'), and blocked errors alike — after which the emailValid check (lines 69-74) permanently reports that email invalid for the rest of the session, with nothing ever clearing the list. A user who submits an email that is already registered gets 'email invalid' on that field forever after (even if the conflict was transient and the server would accept a retry), and must reload the page to recover; additionally the server's specific reason in user.errors.full_messages is discarded and replaced with the generic I18n 'user.email.invalid' message, so the user cannot tell a typo from a ban from a duplicate.

[ADVISORY] The spec for the new EmailValidator only exercises the BlockedEmail branch (with should_block? stubbed out) and never exercises the whitelist/blacklist branches (lines 4-12 of lib/validators/email_validator.rb) that were just relocated from User#email_validator into this new class. A regression in the migrated domain-restriction logic (e.g., the regex construction in email_in_restriction_setting?, or the elsif precedence that makes blacklist ignored whenever a whitelist is set) passes the entire test suite introduced in this diff; since this is a fresh file, the copy could drift from the original semantics with no failing spec.

[ADVISORY] No test in the diff verifies that the User model actually runs the new EmailValidator — there is no model or request spec that creates a User with a real BlockedEmail record and asserts validation failure, so the wiring `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` is unverified end-to-end. The blocked_email_spec and email_validator_spec each test their unit in isolation with stubs, so a regression that disconnects the feature (validator misregistered under the `email:` key, the `if: :email_changed?` condition removed, or the line deleted) would leave every test in this diff green while signups with blocked emails are silently accepted again — the PR's core behavior has zero integration verification.

[ADVISORY] The new errors/values response payload added to UsersController#create has no spec coverage anywhere in the diff, despite the client-side rejection flow depending on its exact shape (`result.errors.email` and `result.values.email` in create_account_controller.js:274). A regression in the payload (renaming `values`, dropping the email key from the slice, or `to_hash` shape changes across Rails versions) silently disables the client-side rejection feedback — the user gets only the generic flash message and the rejectedEmails pre-validation never engages — with no failing test to catch it.

[ADVISORY] The values payload echoes back `name` and `username` in addition to `email`, but the only consumer in this diff (create_account_controller.js:275) reads `result.values.email` exclusively, making two of the three fields dead payload on the error contract. Every future reader of this response contract must guess whether name/username are consumed by some client; the implied-but-unused fields invite divergence the next time the error shape changes (a consumer updated for 'values' cannot tell which keys are load-bearing).

[BUG] The blocked_emails feature ships with no writer anywhere in the diff: no admin controller, route, UI, rake task, or seed creates BlockedEmail rows, so the table starts and stays empty. The stated intent ('comprehensive email validation for blocked users') never fires in practice — no operator can block an email without manual SQL inserts (the spec's own comment at spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb line 16 concedes this: 'If we manually load the table with some emails'). Under-scoped: the enforcement half of the feature is merged with no usable provisioning half.

[ADVISORY] The action_type :do_nothing value and the match_count/last_match_at columns are written but never read by any code in this diff — dead schema surface with no consumer. Future readers and schema consumers must reason about a two-action state machine (:do_nothing) that no code path can ever produce, plus telemetry columns (match_count, last_match_at) nothing reports on; whoever adds the missing admin UI inherits an unwritten contract about what :do_nothing records mean and whether do_nothing matches should still increment statistics (should_block? currently increments even when it returns false).

[ADVISORY] The new failure payload echoes name and username back to the client (values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")) and exposes the full validation error hash, but the only consumer in this diff reads result.values.email and result.errors.email. API surface expands beyond the requirement with untraceable fields; every failed signup now returns a structured dump of all validation errors (a de facto public API contract) that future client or third-party code will depend on before any requirement defined it, constraining later changes to user error handling.

[ADVISORY] rejectedEmails caches every server-side email rejection — not just blocked-email rejections — and the cache never expires for the controller's lifetime. Any email validation failure (format, whitelist/blacklist) puts the address in rejectedEmails; if an admin removes a block (or fixes a misconfigured blacklist) while the user still has the modal open, the user's resubmission of the same address is rejected client-side at lines 69-75 with no server round-trip, showing 'invalid' indefinitely until a full page reload — the client-side state cannot be reconciled with server state within the session.

[ADVISORY] The new spec stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and exercises only the blocked-email branch; the whitelist/blacklist restriction logic moved verbatim from User#email_validator into EmailValidator has no test coverage in this diff. A regression in email_in_restriction_setting? (e.g., the unescaped-domain regex at lib/validators/email_validator.rb line 19, whose dot-gsub behavior was previously covered under whatever exercised the old User validator, now moved with changed call signature value vs self.email) would pass the suite; the behavior-bearing relocation is untested in its new home.

[ADVISORY] should_block? performs a read-modify-write (increment match_count, save) inside an ActiveModel validation, so the blocked-email lookup is a synchronous DB write on every signup email validation. Every registration attempt with a matching blocked email takes a row lock and write inside the request-critical validation path; concurrent signups from the same blocked address serialize on the row, and a save failure (e.g., unique-index race on a simultaneously inserted record) raises inside validation and surfaces as a 500 instead of a 4xx rejection.

[BUG] should_block? increments match_count via a non-atomic read-modify-write (record.match_count += 1; record.save), so concurrent validations of the same blocked email lose updates. Two simultaneous signup attempts with the same blocked email both read match_count=N and both write N+1, so the counter undercounts and last_match_at can be stale; the fix is an atomic UPDATE (BlockedEmail.update_counters / update_all("match_count = match_count + 1")), not instance read-modify-write. Additionally record.save without a bang silently swallows save failures, dropping the stat with no signal.

[BUG] The blocklist lookup BlockedEmail.where(email: email) compares the raw submitted email case-sensitively against the stored entry, and no path in this diff downcases either side before the comparison. An admin who stores 'Spam@x.com' (the only writer is manual/console entry, so no normalization is applied anywhere) does not block signups with 'spam@x.com' — the block is bypassed by a case variant. The same gap affects the unique index on email (db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb line 11), which is case-sensitive in PostgreSQL, so 'a@x.com' and 'A@x.com' both insert as distinct rows; the lookup and uniqueness control need a canonical form (downcase on write and a lower(email) unique index/lookup).

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table ships with no writer anywhere in this diff: no admin controller, UI route, rake task, or seed path creates BlockedEmail records. Operators cannot actually populate the blocklist through the application; until a management path lands, the feature is inert outside the rails console, and the spec fabricator is the only code that creates rows.

[ADVISORY] The validator is side-effectful and non-idempotent: validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which performs a DB write (match_count increment, last_match_at update) inside a validation pass. Every User save where email_changed? re-runs the write, so match_count does not count blocked signup attempts — it counts validation passes, including admin/profile email changes, repeated saves, and any request where the record is validated more than once; a blocked email whose action is :do_nothing still incurs a write on every validation. Validation logic should be pure; the stat write belongs in the controller/create path.

[ADVISORY] The new client-side short-circuit for rejected emails reports the generic I18n 'user.email.invalid' reason, discarding the specific server-side 'user.email.blocked' message the server just returned. A user whose email was blocked by the admin sees 'email is invalid' on retry — a format complaint — when the actual cause is a policy block, sending them to fix a typo that does not exist; the server message is available in result.message/errors at the push site (lines 274-276) but is not carried into the cached validation.

[ADVISORY] The refactor repurposes the `email: true` validator slot for domain whitelist/blacklist and blocked-email table lookups under a class named EmailValidator that performs no email-format validation at all. The PR's stated objective ('comprehensive email validation') silently drifted during iteration: a reader of `validates :email, email: true` — the conventional Rails idiom for format checking — concludes format is validated when it is not, and any other model that adopts `email: true` inherits a DB-table read plus a stat-mutating write (BlockedEmail.should_block?) as a validation side effect. The old private `validate :email_validator` coupling was explicit; the new coupling is hidden behind an option name that means something else.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table, model, and validation wiring ship with no writer anywhere in the diff — no admin UI, controller action, rake task, or seed path can create a BlockedEmail record. Operators cannot actually block an email address without inserting rows via console/SQL by hand, so the PR's headline intent ('email validation for blocked users') is not reachable through the product; the feature is inert until a follow-up that nobody has accepted yet.

[ADVISORY] should_block? is a predicate that performs a database write (match_count increment, last_match_at update, record.save) inside model validation, and the validator skips it entirely when a prior error exists on the attribute. Any `valid?` call on a User with a changed email (not just registration) increments match statistics, inflating counters from unrelated validation paths; and because EmailValidator only calls should_block? when `record.errors[attribute].blank?`, whether a match is recorded depends on validation ordering — a blocked email that also fails the domain check is never counted, so the stats the spec relies on are silently incomplete.

[BUG] The blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email)`) while the domain-restriction regex in the same validator is compiled case-insensitive (`Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)`), so a blocked address submitted with different casing is not blocked. A registration for 'Spam@Spammers.org' passes should_block? when 'spam@spammers.org' is in blocked_emails, defeating the feature's core intent for the simplest possible evasion; the case-insensitive flag on the domain check in the same file shows case was an accepted constraint that the new lookup silently dropped.

[ADVISORY] Every test in the new spec stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? entirely, and no test in the diff exercises the real integration: the User model's `email: true` wiring, the should_block? DB round-trip during validation, or the controller's new errors/values failure payload that the client's rejectedEmails flow depends on. A regression in the payload contract (e.g. `result.errors.email` or `result.values.email` keys in users_controller.rb:197-200) breaks the client-side rejection feedback silently, because the only code path that produces and consumes those keys is never covered; likewise a broken BlockedEmail query inside the validator would pass this spec.

[ADVISORY] rejectedEmails caches the server-echoed value (`result.values.email`) but the guard compares it against the raw client-typed `accountEmail`, and once pushed the rejection persists for the whole modal session with duplicates accumulating on repeated failed submissions. If the server normalizes the email (e.g. downcases it) the cached value never matches the typed value and the client-side guard never fires; conversely, if an admin lifts the block while the modal is open, the user stays locked out of a now-valid email until they reopen the modal, since nothing ever removes an entry from rejectedEmails.

[BUG] The domain whitelist/blacklist regex `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` is unanchored, so an email whose local part ends and real domain begins with an allowlisted suffix passes the whitelist check. With email_domains_whitelist set to e.g. 'gmail.com', an attacker registering as 'attacker@gmail.com.evil.net' matches `@gmail\.com` as a substring even though their actual receiving domain is evil.net, letting them create accounts from a domain the admin explicitly excluded (the same unanchoring also over-blocks on the blacklist side, e.g. 'user@gmail.com.evil.net' is rejected as a gmail address). The regexp is only correct if anchored to the end of the local@domain boundary.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up the email with an exact-case `BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` and no downcase normalization, so the blocklist is bypassed by changing letter case. An admin blocks 'bad@spammers.org'; an anonymous attacker signs up as 'BAD@SPAMMERS.ORG' (or any case permutation), the exact-match lookup misses, and the registration succeeds — the blocking control silently fails for every non-identically-cased variant, while the Rails uniqueness check treats the cased variant as a distinct account so nothing else stops it.

[ADVISORY] The admin-set whitelist/blacklist setting is compiled straight into Regexp.new with only '.' escaped, so regex metacharacters in the setting are interpreted as pattern syntax and malformed settings raise RegexpError at signup time. A blacklist entry containing an unbalanced '(' or '[' (a plausible admin typo) raises Regexp.new → RegexpError inside validate_each on every account-creation attempt, returning a 500 for all signups until the setting is fixed; entries with quantifier characters (e.g. 'foo+bar.com') silently match different addresses than the admin intended. This is a config-backed sink where admin configuration is treated as trusted regex source.

[ADVISORY] should_block? performs a read-modify-write (match_count += 1, save) inside validate_each, so every validation of a changed email — triggered by unauthenticated signup attempts — issues a DB query and, on match, an unauthenticated UPDATE. An anonymous attacker hammering the signup endpoint with a blocked email forces one UPDATE per request (write amplification / cheap DB-load DoS), and the non-atomic read-modify-write races under concurrent requests silently losing match_count increments, corrupting the admin's block-hit statistics; validators are also expected to be side-effect-free, so this write fires in any future context that runs the email validator, not just registration.

[ADVISORY] The unauthenticated signup error response now distinguishes the per-email blocklist rejection ('is not allowed.') from the domain whitelist/blacklist rejection ('is not allowed from that email provider...'), letting anonymous callers enumerate which specific addresses are on the admin's private blocklist. An attacker can probe candidate addresses one by one against /users and read the errors.email message text to determine blocklist membership — information previously hidden inside a generic joined error string — which is reconnaissance value when the blocklist encodes known-abuse contacts or investigated addresses.

[ADVISORY] The EmailValidator spec stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? in both examples and never exercises the whitelist/blacklist domain branches of validate_each, so the majority of the new validator's logic has zero coverage in this diff. The migrated domain-restriction logic (email_in_restriction_setting?, the `if errors.blank?` guard that suppresses the blocked check when a domain error already exists) can regress silently: the two examples pass even if the whitelist branch, the blacklist branch, or the error-precedence ordering is broken, because should_block? is the only path the stubbed tests touch. The real DB-backed integration between EmailValidator and BlockedEmail is never tested anywhere in the diff (spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb tests should_block? in isolation, never through the validator).

[ADVISORY] The example 'returns false if a record with the email doesn't exist' uses `should be_false`, which in this RSpec era matches any falsey value including nil, while should_block? actually returns nil (not false) when no record exists due to `record && record.action_type == actions[:block]` short-circuiting to nil. The test name claims the method 'returns false' but the assertion passes for nil, so a future refactor that changes the return contract (e.g., a caller distinguishing nil from false, or the method accidentally returning nil in the matched-record path) would not be caught by this spec; the test verifies falsey-ness, not the documented boolean contract.

[ADVISORY] The new `errors:` and `values:` fields added to the failed-registration JSON response have no test in this diff (I checked the only test files changed here — spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb, spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb, spec/fabricators/blocked_email_fabricator.rb — none reference UsersController or its create action). The client-side rejectedEmails mechanism in create_account_controller.js depends on exactly this response shape (`result.errors.email` present AND `result.values.email` present); a regression in the controller's error payload (e.g., `values` omitted or keys renamed) breaks the blocked-email UX silently, and no spec in this diff would catch it — the frontend code would push `undefined` into rejectedEmails, which `.contains(email)` then never matches, permanently disabling the client-side rejection display.

[ADVISORY] The User model's email validation was rewired from the deleted email_validator method to the new EmailValidator (adding the BlockedEmail lookup to every user save with email_changed?), with no test change in this diff covering blocked-email rejection at the User level. The user-facing behavior promised by the PR title — a blocked email being rejected at registration — is only verified through the validator's stubbed unit spec and BlockedEmail's own spec; the actual wiring (User.new(email: blocked).valid? returning false with the 'is not allowed.' message) is untested, so a miswired attribute option (e.g., the `if: :email_changed?` guard interacting with the presence/uniqueness split on lines 45-46) would pass the whole suite while blocking nothing in production.

[ADVISORY] The new client-side rejectedEmails state machine (pushObject on failed signup, membership check in emailValidated, and the new `rejectedEmails.@each` dependent key) has no test change in this diff referencing it. The rejection-retry UX branch (`if (this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email))` returning a failed InputValidation before the authOptions check) can silently regress — e.g., the `.contains()` check fires for a user retrying a valid-but-typo'd email or never fires because values.email casing differs from what the user typed — and no qunit or spec change in this diff exercises either the pushObject side or the contains side, so both the new if-branch and the new observer key are dead code as far as this diff's tests can prove.

[ADVISORY] The migration creates the blocked_emails table but no writer exists anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, controller, rake task, or seed path inserts rows, so the table ships empty and EmailValidator's BlockedEmail.should_block? branch can never fire in production. Operators get a schema change (and the per-signup match_count write path) with no way to actually block an email; the feature is dead code until a separate change adds a management surface, and the table's unique index and NOT NULL constraints were deployed before being exercised by anything but specs.

[BUG] The client permanently blacklists any email that produced ANY :email validation error — not just admin-blocked emails — because `result.errors.email` is truthy for uniqueness races, whitelist/blacklist rejections, and blocked-email errors alike, and rejectedEmails has no removal or re-validation path. A user whose signup fails for a transient email error (e.g., two concurrent signups racing the unique index, so one gets a uniqueness error on :email) has that valid email pushed into rejectedEmails; every subsequent attempt in the session shows the field as failed without a server round-trip, even though the server would now accept it. The only recovery is a full page reload, and the inline message ('invalid') misdirects the user about what went wrong.

[BUG] The rejected-email path reports the state with I18n.t('user.email.invalid'), which misdescribes the operation — the email is admin-blocked, not syntactically or policy-'invalid' — while the flash simultaneously shows the server's correct message ('is not allowed.'), so the UI presents two contradictory explanations for the same failure. A user whose email was blocked sees 'email invalid' under the field and 'not allowed' in the flash; debugging the discrepancy wastes support cycles, and users with a legitimately blocked address keep 'fixing' a format that was never wrong.

[ADVISORY] should_block? uses a non-atomic read-modify-write (`record.match_count += 1; record.save`) with no lock or atomic UPDATE, so concurrent signup attempts against the same blocked email lose increments. Under a burst of signup attempts with the same blocked address (the exact scenario match_count exists to measure), two requests read the same count and the last write wins — match_count undercounts and last_match_at can be stale, silently corrupting the admin telemetry this table was built for.

[ADVISORY] The return value of `record.save` is ignored, so a failed statistics write is silently swallowed while should_block? still returns its block decision. If the stats UPDATE fails (e.g., the row was deleted between the SELECT and the save), the block decision is still enforced but the match is never recorded — the admin's block-hit log silently loses entries with no log line or error anywhere.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table is ships-inert: nothing in this diff writes a BlockedEmail row — there is no admin controller, UI action, rake task, seed, or site-setting path — so the blocklist can only be populated by direct database inserts. Operators deploying this feature get a validation hook that always queries an empty table; the 'comprehensive email validation' silently does nothing in production until someone hand-crafts SQL, and there is no supported way to unblock or audit entries later.

[ADVISORY] rejectedEmails is initialized per controller instantiation and only ever appended to, with no clearing on success, navigation, or blocklist change, so client-side rejections outlive the server state that produced them. After an admin removes a block (or a false positive is fixed server-side), any user who already hit the rejection in the same session keeps seeing the email field as failed on this form until they happen to reload the page; duplicate pushObject calls on repeated failures also grow the array unboundedly within the session.

This is an incompleteness/scope issue rather than a correctness regression (existing behavior still works with an empty table).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The domain whitelist/blacklist regex `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` is unanchored, so an email whose local part ends and real domain begins with an allowlisted suffix passes the whitelist check. With email_domains_whitelist set to e.g. 'gmail.com', an attacker registering as 'attacker@gmail.com.evil.net' matches `@gmail\.com` as a substring even though their actual receiving domain is evil.net, letting them create accounts from a domain the admin explicitly excluded (the same unanchoring also over-blocks on the blacklist side, e.g. 'user@gmail.com.evil.net' is rejected as a gmail address). The regexp is only correct if anchored to the end of the local@domain boundary.
matched_golden_ids: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Yes. Both describe the same underlying vulnerability: the regex `@(#{domains})` is not properly anchored to the end of the domain, so it matches allowlisted domain strings as substrings within a longer domain (e.g., `gmail.com.evil.net` / `evil.example.com`), enabling whitelist bypass (and also causing blacklist over-matching).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up the email with an exact-case `BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` and no downcase normalization, so the blocklist is bypassed by changing letter case. An admin blocks 'bad@spammers.org'; an anonymous attacker signs up as 'BAD@SPAMMERS.ORG' (or any case permutation), the exact-match lookup misses, and the registration succeeds — the blocking control silently fails for every non-identically-cased variant, while the Rails uniqueness check treats the cased variant as a distinct account so nothing else stops it.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the lookup is `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` with no normalization (e.g., `downcase`) or case-insensitive query. The `blocked_emails.email` column is a plain `string` with a unique index (`add_index :blocked_emails, :email, unique: true`), and the model validation is `uniqueness: true` without `case_sensitive: false`, so nothing in this diff guarantees case-insensitive matching. Therefore, a differently-cased input email can bypass the block check as described (case-sensitivity depends on DB/collation, but the code itself is case-sensitive).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The admin-set whitelist/blacklist setting is compiled straight into Regexp.new with only '.' escaped, so regex metacharacters in the setting are interpreted as pattern syntax and malformed settings raise RegexpError at signup time. A blacklist entry containing an unbalanced '(' or '[' (a plausible admin typo) raises Regexp.new → RegexpError inside validate_each on every account-creation attempt, returning a 500 for all signups until the setting is fixed; entries with quantifier characters (e.g. 'foo+bar.com') silently match different addresses than the admin intended. This is a config-backed sink where admin configuration is treated as trusted regex source.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `EmailValidator#email_in_restriction_setting?`, the admin-provided `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist/blacklist` is interpolated into `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` after only `.` is escaped (`domains = setting.gsub('.', '\\.')`). Other regex metacharacters (e.g., `(`, `[`, `+`, `?`, `|`) are not escaped, so malformed settings can raise `RegexpError` during `validate_each` and valid-but-unescaped settings can match unintended domains. This behavior is directly present in `lib/validators/email_validator.rb` in the diff and is executed during signup validation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] should_block? performs a read-modify-write (match_count += 1, save) inside validate_each, so every validation of a changed email — triggered by unauthenticated signup attempts — issues a DB query and, on match, an unauthenticated UPDATE. An anonymous attacker hammering the signup endpoint with a blocked email forces one UPDATE per request (write amplification / cheap DB-load DoS), and the non-atomic read-modify-write races under concurrent requests silently losing match_count increments, corrupting the admin's block-hit statistics; validators are also expected to be side-effect-free, so this write fires in any future context that runs the email validator, not just registration.
matched_golden_ids: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Yes. The candidate flags that `should_block?`/email validation performs a read-modify-write (increments `match_count` and saves) during what should be a side-effect-free check/validation. It explicitly mentions race conditions under concurrency and corruption of block-hit statistics, aligning with the golden issue about side effects during a read operation and misleading behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The unauthenticated signup error response now distinguishes the per-email blocklist rejection ('is not allowed.') from the domain whitelist/blacklist rejection ('is not allowed from that email provider...'), letting anonymous callers enumerate which specific addresses are on the admin's private blocklist. An attacker can probe candidate addresses one by one against /users and read the errors.email message text to determine blocklist membership — information previously hidden inside a generic joined error string — which is reconnaissance value when the blocklist encodes known-abuse contacts or investigated addresses.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a per-address blocklist (BlockedEmail / EmailValidator) that adds a distinct validation message `I18n.t('user.email.blocked')` ("is not allowed.") versus the existing domain allow/deny message `user.email.not_allowed` ("is not allowed from that email provider..."). This makes it straightforward for an anonymous caller to POST candidate emails to `/users` and distinguish blocklist membership by inspecting `errors.email` (or the rendered `message`), which is an information-disclosure/security regression enabled by this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The client permanently blacklists any email that produced ANY :email validation error — not just admin-blocked emails — because `result.errors.email` is truthy for uniqueness races, whitelist/blacklist rejections, and blocked-email errors alike, and rejectedEmails has no removal or re-validation path. A user whose signup fails for a transient email error (e.g., two concurrent signups racing the unique index, so one gets a uniqueness error on :email) has that valid email pushed into rejectedEmails; every subsequent attempt in the session shows the field as failed without a server round-trip, even though the server would now accept it. The only recovery is a full page reload, and the inline message ('invalid') misdirects the user about what went wrong.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does add a client-side cache `rejectedEmails` that unconditionally records any failed signup response where `result.errors.email` is present (`create_account_controller.js`), and thereafter short-circuits email validation for that exact string with a generic `user.email.invalid` message (no removal/refresh path, and dependency is `rejectedEmails.@each`). This is grounded: it conflates all server-side email validation failures (blocked, domain restrictions, uniqueness, etc.) into a permanent-in-session local rejection and can mislead by showing "invalid" instead of the real server reason. However, the finding’s key claim that this will wrongly block a now-valid email due to a transient uniqueness race is not directly verifiable from the diff (most email errors are likely to remain errors on retry), so it’s better classified as a significant design/UX/edge-case concern rather than a proven defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The rejected-email path reports the state with I18n.t('user.email.invalid'), which misdescribes the operation — the email is admin-blocked, not syntactically or policy-'invalid' — while the flash simultaneously shows the server's correct message ('is not allowed.'), so the UI presents two contradictory explanations for the same failure. A user whose email was blocked sees 'email invalid' under the field and 'not allowed' in the flash; debugging the discrepancy wastes support cycles, and users with a legitimately blocked address keep 'fixing' a format that was never wrong.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, once an email is added to `rejectedEmails`, `emailValidation` always fails with `reason: I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` (new early-return). But the email can be rejected for other server-side reasons (e.g. new `EmailValidator` adds `user.email.blocked` / `user.email.not_allowed`), and the server response now includes `message` built from `user.errors.full_messages` plus `errors`/`values`. The failure handler pushes the email into `rejectedEmails` for any `result.errors.email`, so a blocked/not_allowed email will subsequently show the field error as “invalid” while the flash shows the server’s “not allowed” message, creating contradictory UI for the same failure.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] should_block? uses a non-atomic read-modify-write (`record.match_count += 1; record.save`) with no lock or atomic UPDATE, so concurrent signup attempts against the same blocked email lose increments. Under a burst of signup attempts with the same blocked address (the exact scenario match_count exists to measure), two requests read the same count and the last write wins — match_count undercounts and last_match_at can be stale, silently corrupting the admin telemetry this table was built for.

adjudication.rationale: In app/models/blocked_email.rb, `should_block?` does `record = BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` then `record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now; record.save`. This is a non-atomic read-modify-write with no locking/transaction or atomic `UPDATE`, so concurrent requests matching the same email can overwrite each other’s increments and timestamps (lost update), undercounting `match_count` and potentially leaving `last_match_at` stale.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The return value of `record.save` is ignored, so a failed statistics write is silently swallowed while should_block? still returns its block decision. If the stats UPDATE fails (e.g., the row was deleted between the SELECT and the save), the block decision is still enforced but the match is never recorded — the admin's block-hit log silently loses entries with no log line or error anywhere.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, when a matching record is found it increments `match_count`/`last_match_at` and calls `record.save` but ignores its return value (and doesn’t handle failure). The method’s return (`record && record.action_type == actions[:block]`) is independent of whether the stats write succeeds, so a failed save would indeed block (or not) based on `action_type` while silently not recording the hit. The diff doesn’t prove `save` will realistically fail in normal operation, but the finding is grounded in the shown code path and highlights a real robustness/observability gap in the newly added stats tracking.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table is ships-inert: nothing in this diff writes a BlockedEmail row — there is no admin controller, UI action, rake task, seed, or site-setting path — so the blocklist can only be populated by direct database inserts. Operators deploying this feature get a validation hook that always queries an empty table; the 'comprehensive email validation' silently does nothing in production until someone hand-crafts SQL, and there is no supported way to unblock or audit entries later.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds the `blocked_emails` table/model and wires it into validation (`EmailValidator` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`), but there is no code path in this diff that creates/updates `BlockedEmail` rows in normal app operation (no controller/admin UI/seed/rake task/etc.). As a result, in a default deployment the table will remain empty and the new blocking behavior won’t take effect unless operators manually insert rows, and there’s no supported management/auditing surface added here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] rejectedEmails is initialized per controller instantiation and only ever appended to, with no clearing on success, navigation, or blocklist change, so client-side rejections outlive the server state that produced them. After an admin removes a block (or a false positive is fixed server-side), any user who already hit the rejection in the same session keeps seeing the email field as failed on this form until they happen to reload the page; duplicate pushObject calls on repeated failures also grow the array unboundedly within the session.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` to the controller and appends to it on failed create responses (`pushObject(result.values.email)`), then makes `emailValidation` immediately fail client-side if `rejectedEmails.contains(email)`. There is no clearing/deduping logic shown on success or subsequent attempts, so within the lifetime of that controller instance the list can grow and can cause a previously-rejected email to be treated as invalid without re-checking the server. However, the claim about "navigation"/session persistence and blocklist changes cannot be fully verified from this diff alone (controller lifecycle isn’t shown), making it more of a state-management/UX concern than a guaranteed broken behavior.
